_comment: Example `<target>/.crustify/alloc.json` produced by `CrustifyAllocAnalyzer`. Catalogues a codebase's allocator surface (Phase 0.3 of the C-to-Rust porting plan) as a machine-parseable allocator universe. Four top-level categories - `allocators`, `duplicators`, `refcounts`, `locks` - plus a small `cleansers` list for standalone zero-without-free primitives. Downstream consumers: the buffer pass of `CrustifyTypeAnalyzer` (synthesizes `string` / `array` cluster entries in types.json), the strings/arrays type-wrapper prompts, and lifecycle classification (refcount-field / lock-field recognition). Values below are GENERIC - libc primitives (universal) plus a fictional `proj_*` / `PROJ_*` project-wrapper layer that illustrates every archetype's JSON shape without committing to any one codebase's naming. A real run substitutes the target project's actual symbols; one cluster per archetype found, not one per call-site.
_comment_syms_base: Every primitive (alloc, free, copy, refcount op, lock op, refcount type, lock type) carries the **syms.json base shape**: `{name, kind, linked_in, declared_in[], defined_in, type}`. The `kind` field uses the same 10-value taxonomy as syms.json (function_{exported,static,inline_header,inline_tu}, macro_{constant,symbol,typegen,misc}, global_{static,extern}) and is `null` for typedefs/structs that aren't classifiable as a `kind` (plain typedefs, struct declarations). External symbols (libc, pthread, ...) carry `defined_in: null` with `declared_in` populated. `linked_in` is composer-emitted null; future link-time attribution may fill it. Downstream agents resolve any primitive against the syms tree by walking `<repo_root>/.crustify/analysis/<defined_in-stem>/syms.json` (or `<declared_in[0]>-stem>/syms.json` when defined_in is null).
_comment_macro_variants: **Decision**: macro variants (e.g. a `PROJ_malloc(n)` user-facing macro that expands to `proj_malloc(n, __FILE__, __LINE__)`) appear as their own clusters. There is **no `expands_to` field** - macro clusters stand alone. The agent enumerates both the macro family and the underlying function family when both are real call sites in port-scope code; downstream type-wrapper prompts pick whichever the codebase actually calls (Rust FFI typically targets the function, not the macro). This keeps each cluster a self-contained allocation/release pairing the buffer agent can match against.
_comment_allocators: **Category 1.** One cluster per (alloc-routine, free-routine) pair. Booleans `zeroing` (alloc zero-fills, true for zalloc/calloc), `clearing` (free zeroes the buffer before releasing, true for clear-free variants), `sized` (alloc takes `(count, size)` and overflow-checks: true for `*_array` variants and calloc - these are **separate clusters** from the base `*_malloc`, not folded in, so the buffer pass can ambiguously identify each `{alloc, free}` pair), `aligned` (alloc honours an alignment argument). `family` is a free-form grouping string (e.g. `libc`, `<projname>`, `<projname>_secure`, `<projname>_aligned`). `realloc` and `clear_realloc` are **optional fields on the cluster** carrying a syms-base entry each - they're the resize companions of the alloc/free pair, not a separate category. Omit (or set to null) when the family has no realloc.
_comment_duplicators: **Category 2.** One cluster per copy/dup primitive. Booleans `string` (copies a NUL-terminated string), `sized` (takes an explicit length), `bounded` (memcpy-style bounded copy that doesn't necessarily NUL-terminate), `allocates` (the copy itself allocates the dest: true for `*dup`, false for `memcpy`). `alloc` / `free` are **name-reference strings** into `allocators[*].alloc.name` / `allocators[*].free.name` (e.g. `"proj_malloc"`), or `null` when the copy is caller-owned (memcpy-style). Name references - not full sub-entries - to keep JSON compact; downstream agents resolve the reference back into the `allocators` list for full metadata.
_comment_refcounts: **Category 3.** One cluster per (refcount type, primitive family). Booleans `atomic` (backend uses hardware atomics on the common platform), `has_lock_fallback` (a non-atomic backend uses a lock). `fallback_lock` is a name-reference into `locks[*].type.name` (e.g. `"PROJ_RWLOCK"`) or null. `type` is the syms-base entry for the C type (struct or typedef declaration; `kind: null` is normal). `field_layout` is `{field: <name>, type: <C type>}` describing the in-struct integer field the primitives manipulate (composer hint for the buffer/lifecycle agent; not a full type description). The primitive set: `new`, `up`, `down`, `get`, `free` - each a syms-base entry, all required when present in the codebase. `assert` is an **optional** sanity-check macro (e.g. an `ASSERT_NOT_NEGATIVE`-style guard) for catching double-frees.
_comment_locks: **Category 4.** One cluster per (lock type, primitive family). `kind` is one of `"rwlock"`, `"mutex"`, `"spinlock"`. Booleans `reentrant` (recursive acquisition allowed) and `opaque` (type is opaque to callers - true for `typedef void *` style). `type` carries the syms-base entry for the lock type. Primitives: `new`, `read_lock` (or null when `kind != "rwlock"`), `write_lock` (also acts as the single `lock` for non-rwlock kinds - still called `write_lock` for schema uniformity), `unlock`, `free`. The buffer/lifecycle agent resolves `refcounts[*].fallback_lock` references against this list's `type.name` values.
_comment_cleansers: Standalone zero-without-free primitives (e.g. a `proj_cleanse` that uses a volatile memset to defeat dead-store elimination) - small enough to keep at the top level instead of a full category. One cluster per primitive: `{note, op: <syms-base entry>}`. Used by the buffer pass when a cluster needs a length-aware sensitive-data wipe separate from its dtor.

allocators._comment_example: libc archetype - the universal ground-truth allocator every C project sits atop. Most projects wrap libc behind a `proj_*` layer (see the next cluster) and only the wrapper appears at port-scope call sites; libc itself is still catalogued because some code paths bypass the wrapper. External - `defined_in: null`.
allocators.note: libc malloc/free - the universal ground-truth allocator.

allocators._comment_example: libc zeroing archetype - `calloc` is `zeroing: true` AND `sized: true` (takes `(count, size)`, overflow-checked, zero-fills). One cluster, both flags set; pairs with libc `free`.
allocators.note: libc calloc - overflow-checked, zero-filled array allocator.

allocators._comment_example: Project-wrapper archetype - the typical `proj_*` layer most non-trivial C codebases interpose between source code and libc (debug tracking, dispatch indirection, error reporting). Replace `proj_` with the target's actual prefix (e.g. `CRYPTO_`, `apr_`, `g_`, `xml`, `nspr_`, ...). `realloc` and `clear_realloc` are the optional resize companions.
allocators.note: Primary project allocator layer - wraps libc with debug tracking and a replaceable dispatch table. Every project allocation funnels through this pair unless explicitly using a secure / aligned / array variant.

alloc.name: proj_malloc
alloc.type: void *proj_malloc(size_t num, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_free
free.type: void proj_free(void *ptr, const char *file, int line)

realloc.name: proj_realloc
realloc.type: void *proj_realloc(void *addr, size_t num, const char *file, int line)

clear_realloc.name: proj_clear_realloc
clear_realloc.type: void *proj_clear_realloc(void *addr, size_t old_len, size_t num, const char *file, int line)

allocators._comment_example: Macro form of the project-wrapper archetype - uppercase `PROJ_malloc(n)` expands to `proj_malloc(n, __FILE__, __LINE__)`. Standalone cluster - no `expands_to` linkback to the function-form cluster. `kind: null` because macro kind (constant/symbol/typegen/misc) is body-inspection territory; the agent classifies if downstream needs it. All `type` fields are null (macros carry no signature).
allocators.note: Macro form of the project wrapper layer - appears in C source as `PROJ_malloc(n)`. Not callable from Rust FFI (Rust calls `proj_malloc` directly). Kept as its own cluster so port-scope grep over C source resolves it.

allocators._comment_example: Zeroing archetype - alloc zero-fills before returning. `zeroing: true`. Pairs with the same `proj_free`. No realloc on this cluster - a `proj_zalloc` typically has no companion `proj_zrealloc` (callers grow the buffer through `proj_realloc` and zero the new tail themselves).
allocators.note: Zero-filled project allocator - malloc + memset(0). Standard for struct allocation where every field must start zeroed (the common case for `*_new` constructors).

alloc.name: proj_zalloc
alloc.type: void *proj_zalloc(size_t num, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_free
free.type: void proj_free(void *ptr, const char *file, int line)

allocators._comment_example: Overflow-checked array archetype - alloc takes `(count, size)` and validates count*size doesn't overflow before allocating. `sized: true`. A **separate cluster** from `proj_malloc`, not folded into it - the buffer pass needs an unambiguous (alloc, free) pair per cluster, and `proj_malloc_array(n, sz)` is a distinct call-site shape from `proj_malloc(n)`. Pairs with the same `proj_free`.
allocators.note: Overflow-checked array allocator - multiplies count by size with overflow detection. Used by code paths that allocate `n` elements of `sizeof(T)` where `n` is attacker-influenced.

alloc.name: proj_malloc_array
alloc.type: void *proj_malloc_array(size_t num, size_t size, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_free
free.type: void proj_free(void *ptr, const char *file, int line)

realloc.name: proj_realloc_array
realloc.type: void *proj_realloc_array(void *addr, size_t num, size_t size, const char *file, int line)

allocators._comment_example: Clearing-free archetype - `clearing: true`, free zeroes the buffer before releasing (for sensitive data: keys, secrets, tokens). A separate cluster from `(proj_zalloc, proj_free)` because the drop semantics differ; the buffer pass distinguishes zeroing-drop from plain-drop. Pairs with `proj_zalloc` (sensitive data is almost always zero-initialised first). `clear_realloc` is the resize companion that also cleanses.
allocators.note: Zero-on-free pairing for sensitive buffers. The free cleanses the buffer before releasing. Use for key material, tokens, secrets - anything that must not linger in the heap after deallocation.

alloc.name: proj_zalloc
alloc.type: void *proj_zalloc(size_t num, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_clear_free
free.type: void proj_clear_free(void *ptr, size_t num, const char *file, int line)

clear_realloc.name: proj_clear_realloc
clear_realloc.type: void *proj_clear_realloc(void *addr, size_t old_len, size_t num, const char *file, int line)

allocators._comment_example: Secure-heap archetype - alloc comes from a separate locked-pages region (typically `mlock`'d to defeat swap-to-disk attacks against secret material). A distinct allocator family (`proj_secure`) with its own dtor pair, even when it falls back to `proj_malloc`/`proj_free` internally on uninitialised builds.
allocators.note: Secure-heap allocator - allocates from a locked-pages region intended to defeat swap-to-disk attacks. Falls back to the primary allocator when the secure heap hasn't been initialised.

alloc.name: proj_secure_malloc
alloc.type: void *proj_secure_malloc(size_t num, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_secure_free
free.type: void proj_secure_free(void *ptr, const char *file, int line)

allocators._comment_example: Aligned-allocation archetype - alloc honours an alignment argument. `aligned: true`. The signature often carries a `void **freeptr` out-arg because aligned allocation may return a pointer offset from the actual heap allocation; `freeptr` receives the value to pass to `free`. Pairs with `proj_free` (callers must pass `*freeptr`, not the user pointer).
allocators.note: Aligned allocation. Alignment is typically a power of 2 up to some implementation maximum. `*freeptr` receives the pointer to pass to the dtor.

alloc.name: proj_aligned_alloc
alloc.type: void *proj_aligned_alloc(size_t num, size_t alignment, void **freeptr, const char *file, int line)

free.name: proj_free
free.type: void proj_free(void *ptr, const char *file, int line)

duplicators._comment_example: String-dup archetype - `string: true, allocates: true`. `alloc` and `free` are name-references into the allocator cluster whose dtor pairs with this primitive's output (`proj_malloc` / `proj_free` here - the dup uses `proj_malloc` internally). The buffer agent reads these references to know which `string` cluster the dup belongs to.
duplicators.note: NUL-terminated string duplicator. Internally `proj_malloc` + `memcpy`. NULL-safe (returns NULL on NULL input). Output is owned by the caller and released via `proj_free`.

copy.name: proj_strdup
copy.type: char *proj_strdup(const char *str, const char *file, int line)

duplicators._comment_example: Bounded string-dup - `string: true, sized: true`: copies at most `s` bytes and always NUL-terminates. Still `allocates: true`.
duplicators.note: Bounded string duplicator - like `strdup` but copies at most `s` bytes and always NUL-terminates the result.

copy.name: proj_strndup
copy.type: char *proj_strndup(const char *str, size_t s, const char *file, int line)

duplicators._comment_example: Memory-dup archetype - `sized: true, allocates: true`, `string: false`. Caller passes an explicit length; output is a raw byte buffer.
duplicators.note: Sized memory duplicator. Internally `proj_malloc` + `memcpy`. Typically guards against integer overflow on the size argument.

copy.name: proj_memdup
copy.type: void *proj_memdup(const void *data, size_t siz, const char *file, int line)

duplicators._comment_example: Bounded copy archetype - `bounded: true, allocates: false`. memcpy is caller-owned in both directions - the dest must already exist. Both `alloc` and `free` are `null` because there's no implicit ownership transfer.
duplicators.note: Bounded memcpy. Dest is caller-owned; no allocation, no ownership transfer. Included so the buffer agent can recognise call-sites where data is copied INTO a pre-existing buffer (no new cluster needed).

refcounts._comment_example: Project refcount archetype - the typical hardware-atomic-with-lock-fallback wrapper struct most C codebases use. The wrapped int field is `val`. `atomic: true` is the COMMON-platform truth (C11 atomics, GCC builtins, MSVC intrinsics - whichever the build selects); `has_lock_fallback: true` records that a non-atomic fallback exists using a lock. `fallback_lock` is the name-reference into the `locks` list below. All primitives are typically `static inline` (kind: function_inline_header) - Rust must call them through C wrappers (`wrapper_inlines.c` or equivalent). `assert` carries the optional refcount-sanity macro used in every `*_free` (typically guards against the refcount going negative).
refcounts.note: Project refcount. Wraps an int (atomic on common platforms, lock-protected on the fallback). The standard `*_free` pattern is: NULL check -> DOWN_REF -> assert non-negative -> early-return if i > 0 -> free children -> FREE_REF -> free the struct.

locks._comment_example: Project RWLOCK archetype. `kind: "rwlock"` - has separate `read_lock` and `write_lock`. `opaque: true` because the public type is typically a `typedef void` - callers never see the underlying `pthread_rwlock_t` / `SRWLOCK`. `reentrant: false` (POSIX rwlocks aren't reentrant by default). All primitives are real exported functions (defined per-platform in a `threads_pthread.c` / `threads_win.c` pair), reachable from Rust via bindgen.
locks.note: Project reader-writer lock. Opaque typedef; the underlying implementation is `pthread_rwlock_t` on POSIX, `SRWLOCK` on Windows. Used to protect refcount fallback paths and per-object internal state.

cleansers._comment_example: Standalone cleanse - zero a buffer without freeing it. Often implemented with a volatile function pointer to memset to defeat dead-store-elimination optimisations. Used internally by `*_clear_free` and called directly by code that wants length-aware sensitive-data wipe without giving up the allocation.
cleansers.note: Length-aware sensitive-data wipe. Uses a volatile memset to defeat dead-store-elimination. Does NOT free.
